body.heading: The game show trap
paragraphs: The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the TV show Let's Make a Deal. You face three doors. Behind one is a car; behind the other two, goats. You pick a door — say door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens a different door — say door 3 — always revealing a goat, and offers you the chance to switch to door 2.

Most people feel the remaining two doors must be fifty-fifty, so switching gains nothing. It is one of the most natural feelings in all of probability — and it is wrong. Switching wins two times out of three.

body.heading: The hundred-door version
paragraphs: Still doubtful? Stretch the game. Now there are 100 doors, one car and 99 goats. You pick a door. The host, who knows everything, opens 98 of the other doors, all goats, leaving just one unopened door besides yours. Do you switch now?

Of course you do — your first pick had a 1-in-100 chance, so the surviving door carries the other 99 chances in 100. The three-door game is the same shape, just smaller: your pick was right one time in three, and the host's careful reveal concentrates the other two-thirds onto the single door he left closed.

body.heading: The honest maths
paragraphs: The key is that the host never opens the car door and never opens yours. His choice is not random — it is informed, and information is what moves the odds. If your first pick was a goat (which happens two times in three), the host is forced: there is only one goat door left for him to open, so the remaining door must hide the car, and switching wins.

Only when your first pick was the car itself — one time in three — does switching lose. Try it with three cups and a coin, twenty rounds, always switching, and tally the result. The cups will convince you faster than the argument did.

takeaway: Switching wins two times out of three — your first guess didn't get better; the other door inherited the odds.
